title: The true value of higher education
text:
The Monitor performed a valuable service by publishing “A most precious possession,” two insightful essays in The Home Forum (Oct. 19 Weekly) by David Shribman and Marshall Brooks. Both are powerful testaments to the value of a liberal arts education – drawing the important distinction between being educated and being trained. They help counter the conclusion that the primary purpose of a collegiate education is job preparation or that maybe higher education is not worth what it costs today.
The most important benefit of higher education is to teach students how to think clearly and learn effectively so they can continue thinking and learning throughout their lives. The skills and knowledge prized by the workplace today are constantly changing. Just ask the computer science majors who were told they would be in high demand but can’t find jobs because of the artificial intelligence revolution. The best preparation is a sound general education that will enable students to think and learn their way through the relentless, unpredictable change they must cope with. For example, knowing what has gone before (history) and how to communicate effectively (English and speech) is essential.
Young people and their families should ignore those popular listings of the majors that earn the most upon graduation and during a lifetime, and instead focus on preparing for a fuller and more successful life by learning how to think and keep on learning.
Charles Lindahl
Fullerton, California
